name: Meliaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use the project's single Melia concept to teach bipinnate foliage, a conspicuous staminal tube, and yellow drupes while clearly marking it as an introduced comparison rather than a native anchor.

project_scope.note: The current Master Plant Pool contains only Melia azedarach, an accepted species native to Asia/Australia and introduced in North America. This family lesson is therefore comparison-oriented, not a native-family anchor.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the very large 2- to 3-pinnately compound leaf. In flower, look for 5 petals surrounding a conspicuous dark-purple staminal tube. Confirm with persistent yellow drupes.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Deciduous tree with alternate, usually twice-pinnate or nearly tripinnate leaves; individual leaflets are serrate to crenate.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers in loose panicles, pale lilac to white; filaments are united into a prominent staminal tube, a high-value Meliaceae character.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Fleshy yellow drupe with a hard grooved stone, often persisting after leaf fall.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: For the project learner: lacy bipinnate leaf + purple staminal tube + yellow drupe = Melia/Meliaceae.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole tree → bipinnate leaf → staminal tube → yellow drupe → Ailanthus/Sapindales comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Meliaceae is represented here by one conspicuous introduced tree, so the lesson should be crisp and honest rather than pretend it is a broad local family.

steps.title: 1 · Read the giant lacy compound leaf
steps.look_for: Large alternate leaf divided twice or nearly three times into many serrated leaflets.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates Melia from most local native woody Sapindales at a glance.

steps.title: 2 · Find the staminal tube
steps.look_for: Lavender or whitish petals surrounding a dark purple tube made from fused stamen filaments.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the most diagnostic reproductive teaching feature for the project family.

steps.title: 3 · Confirm the yellow drupe
steps.look_for: Round yellow drupes hanging in clusters, often persisting after leaves drop.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit distinguishes Melia from Ailanthus and many compound-leaved lookalikes.

steps.title: 4 · Mark it as introduced
steps.look_for: Melia azedarach is accepted but native to Asia/Australia, not a Central Texas native anchor.
steps.why_it_matters: Keeps ecological teaching aligned with the user's native-landscape goals.

comparisons.title: Meliaceae vs Simaroubaceae
comparisons.rule: Melia has 2–3-pinnate serrated leaves, a conspicuous staminal tube and yellow drupes. Ailanthus has once-pinnate leaves with basal glandular teeth and large clusters of winged samaras.

comparisons.title: Meliaceae vs Sapindaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can be compound-leaved Sapindales, but the Melia staminal tube + persistent yellow drupe combination is distinctive.

visual_lesson.caveat: This module is an introduced-comparison lesson; do not use Melia as a native Central Texas family anchor.

part_specific_photo_handoff.plain: one leaf divided into branches and leaflets
part_specific_photo_handoff.formal: bipinnate or tripinnate compound leaf; rachis, pinnae, pinnules
part_specific_photo_handoff.photo_role: entire compound leaf with branch attachments visible
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Show the distinction between a leaflet and a pinna; count orders of branching.

part_specific_photo_handoff.plain: purple tube holding the pollen organs
part_specific_photo_handoff.photo_role: face and side macro of fresh flower
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Identify fused filaments separately from petals and central style; do not infer from flower color.

part_specific_photo_handoff.plain: yellow fleshy fruit with a hard pit
part_specific_photo_handoff.photo_role: ripe fruit intact and cut open, compared with Ailanthus samara
part_specific_photo_handoff.caption_goal: Contrast the fleshy drupe and stony endocarp with the dry winged samara of Ailanthus.

genera.fast_cue: 2–3-pinnate leaf + purple staminal tube + yellow drupe

taxonomy_notes: Melia azedarach is accepted under current Kew and is native to tropical/subtropical Asia through northern/eastern Australia; it is introduced in North America.

visual_targets.annotation_goal: label rachis, pinnae and ultimate leaflets
separate family recognition from native-landscape recommendation
